essays.answer:
(1) Subject Matter Jurisdiction

The issue is whether the woman's actions in State A constitute a change of domicile. 

A federal court is a court of limited subject matter jurisdiction. Subject matter jurisdiction may be satisfied by either federal question jurisdiction (the claim arises under federal law and appears on the face of the plaintiff's complaint) or by diversity jurisdiction. Because these are state law claims, they do not arise under federal law, and federal question jurisdicition is not proper. That leaves subject matter jurisdiction, which requires complete diversity of citizenship among parties (no plaintiff is domiciled in the same state as any defendant at the time the complaint is filed) and the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000. An amount in controversey is measured by the amount of damages the plaintiff asks for in her complaint, so long as it is brought in good faith and there is not sufficient evidence the plaintiff won't be able to recover the full amount.

Here, there is complete diversity of citizsenship. (i) A corportation is domiciled wherever it is incorporated and where it's principal place of business is (ordinarily, it's headquarters/'nerve center'/where corporate leadership directs, commands, or controls business operations); (ii) A citizen is domiciled in the state that is their permanent and true home. Lastly, a citizen may only change domicile where they have (1) physical presence in the new state, with (2) an intent to remain. At the time of filing, the airline is incorporated and has it's headquarters within state B. The airlines facility in State C does not constitute domicile, since it is only a transportation and maintenance facility, and not somewhere corproate leadership directs, commands, or controls the business. It also is not important that the airline does not serve State B, since the business's headquarters is domiciled there and contains it's headquarters. Also at the time of filing, the woman is physically present in State C, where her permanent home is. These facts, alone, satisfy domicile. While she may argue that because she intends to move to State A, and even signed for an apartment there with the intent to return, she is nevertheless not phyiscally present with the intent to remain. 

Also in this case, the amount in controversy is satisfied. The woman's complaint was for $1 million in damages. This exceeds the 'more than $75,000' threshold required for a case sitting in diversity. Further, she is like making this complaint in good faith, because she suffered serious injuries, and there is no evidence that an airline could not afford to pay these damages. Therefore, subject matter jurisdiction is satisfied because there is complete diversity of citizsenship and the amount in controversy requirement is met. 


(2) Personal Jurisdiction

The issue here is whether State B has jurisdiction over the defendant. Even where a corporation has purposefully availed itself of a state in the course of it's ordinary, far-reaching business activities, if the corporation's minimum contacts are not related to the claim, the forum state has no personal jurisdiction over the defendant. 

Here, the plaintiff filed a complaint in State B and the airline responded with a motion to dismiss in it's first answer, and therefore the motion was properly filed (as opposed to waived, which occurs when the defendant fails to raise the issue in it's first answer or within 30 days of receiving service). The appropriate test the court will apply to determine whether the court has personal jurisdiction is whether the state has sufficient minimum contacts, that those contacts are related to the claim in this case, and apply the fairness factors. If any element is not met, the court will not find personal jursidiction and the proper remedy is dismissal. 

Further, the airline has minimum contacts within the state but these contacts are not sufficiently related to the claim, and therefore the motion to dismiss should be granted. The airline's business operations and headquarters demonstrate the state has purposefully availed itself of the laws of State B and it is foreseeable they may be haled into State B's court over claims related to these contacts. However, the relatedness prong is not met. The woman's complaint arises out of an emergency landing that occurred while flying from State A to State C. Not only did this not occur in State B, but the airline does not even service customers within State B. There is no evidence the woman has ever even been to State B. 

Because the accident did not occur there, the airline does not service customers within State B, and there is no other evidence that the airlines operations in State B are rationally related to the issues arising out of this claim, the court must dismiss for no personal jurisdiction. 

Conclusion

While the court has subject matter jurisdiciton over this claim, the court does not have personal jurisdiction. Because the defendant properly and timely filed a motion to dismiss in their reply to the plaintiff's complaint, the appropriate remedy is dismissal.
essays.model:
***Subject matter jurisdiction.*** The motion to dismiss based on a lack of subject matter jurisdiction should be denied. At issue is whether the woman's actions to move to State A were sufficient to change her citizenship for diversity purposes from State C to State A.

There are two main types of federal subject matter jurisdiction: (1) federal question jurisdiction and (2) diversity of citizenship jurisdiction. Federal question jurisdiction is not available here, as the facts clearly state that the woman's cause of action is a state law tort claim for damages.

Diversity of citizenship jurisdiction requires an amount in controversy of more than $75,000, as determined by the plaintiff's good faith allegation in the complaint, and complete diversity of citizenship, meaning that no plaintiff may share state citizenship with any defendant. A corporation is a citizen of every state in which it is incorporated and the one state in which it has its principal place of business, which the Supreme Court has held to be the place from which the corporation's high level officers direct and control the corporation's activities. For diversity purposes, an individual is a citizen of the state in which she is domiciled, and the party's domicile may be changed by being physically present in the state coupled with the intent to remain there permanently or for an indefinite period.

In the instant case, the amount in controversy is clearly satisfied. The facts state that the woman suffered severe and permanent injuries, and she claims damages in excess of $1 million, and there is no indication that her injuries were minor. In fact, she has missed considerable work time and was hospitalized for three weeks. Regardless of whether she will actually recover $1 million, her damages clearly exceed $75,000 due to the nature and extent of her injuries and the amount of time she missed from work.

Whether complete diversity exists is a more complicated question. On one hand, the citizenship of the airline is simple and easy: it is a citizen only of State A, (1) where its corporate headquarters are located and presumably is the place from which the airline's high level officers direct and control the airline's activities; and (2) where it is incorporated.

The citizenship of the woman, on the other hand, is a bit fuzzy. The facts state that she lived in State C when she bought the ticket. Presumably, she was permanently domiciled in State C at that time. However, the purpose of her trip to State A in September was to sign a lease for an apartment so that she could start a new job in State A in December. Given the timing, it appears that, although the woman was physically present in State A when she rented the apartment, her intent at that time was to go back to State C for a couple of months before making her move to State A permanent. As a result, the woman lacked the intent in September to remain in State A permanently at that time, and thus she continues to be a State C citizen. Had the accident occurred after December, after the woman completed her move, she likely would have been a State A citizen.

What that means is that complete diversity exists. The airline is a citizen of State A, and the woman is a citizen of State C. Accordingly, the motion to dismiss based on subject matter jurisdiction should be denied.

***Personal jurisdiction.*** However, the motion to dismiss based on a lack of personal jurisdiction should be granted. In order to exercise personal jurisdiction over a defendant, the exercise must first be authorized by state statute, and second, the exercise of personal jurisdiction must be constitutional (minimum contacts test).

As to the first point, a federal court must analyze any personal jurisdiction issue as if it were a state court in the jurisdiction. Thus, a federal court in State B will use State B's long arm statute to determine whether it can exercise personal jurisdiction over the airline. Here, State B's long arm statute authorizes personal jurisdiction to the maximum extent permitted by the Constitution. Thus, the two prongs merge together, and the only issue is whether the airline has sufficient minimum contacts with State B such that the exercise of personal jurisdiction over the airline in State B would be fair and reasonable.

If the cause of action arises from or relates to the defendant's contact with the forum, specific jurisdiction—that is, jurisdiction over the defendant for the instant cause of action only—is possible. If the cause of action does not arise from or relate to the the defendant's contacts with the forum, there must be general jurisdiction—that is, personal jurisdiction over the defendant for all causes of action.

In the instant case, the airline's only contact with State B is that it has a facility with 150 employees who take reservations for the airline. This is the facility that the woman used to make the reservation with the airline. However, the instant action sounds in state tort law. The woman's trip was from State C to State A, and the forced landing occurred in State A. Thus, any act of negligence committed by the airline must have occurred in one of those states. The cause of action has nothing to do with any actions by the airline's employees in its reservation center. Furthermore, the airline does not even serve the State B market. As a result, the defendant's activities in State B are unrelated to the airline's contacts with State B. Accordingly, there can be no specific jurisdiction in State B. Nor would it be fair or reasonable to hold the airline accountable in State B when the cause of action did not arise there and its activities in State B are limited.

Given that there is no specific jurisdiction, the court must have general jurisdiction over the airline in order to assert personal jurisdiction over it. In order to be subject to general jurisdiction in a forum state, the defendant must be "at home" in the forum state. To be "at home" in a state, an individual defendant must be domiciled in the state. For a corporation, the United States Supreme Court has stated that the paradigms for being "at home" are the states of incorporation and the state where the corporation has its principal place of business. The Court left open the possibility of there being a third state, but case law makes it clear that in nearly all cases, those two states will be the only two locations where a corporation is "at home" and subject to general personal jurisdiction. Personal jurisdiction also may be exercised when a business registers to do business in the state and state law authorizes personal jurisdiction on this basis.

In the instant case, the facts state that the airline is incorporated in State A and has its principal place of business in State A. The bulk of its operations are in State C, and, as noted above, it does not even serve the State B market. The fact that the airline maintains a call reservation center that employs 150 people in State B does not make it "at home" and subject to general personal jurisdiction in State B. There are also no facts indicating that the airline has registered to do business in State A or that State A's registration statute authorizes PJ on this basis. Accordingly, there is no general personal jurisdiction either.

Because there is no specific or general jurisdiction in State B, the motion to dismiss on the basis of a lack of personal jurisdiction must be granted.
essays.biggestMiss: The whole statutory half of the personal jurisdiction test, then the entire general-jurisdiction analysis: no long-arm statute, no merger of the two prongs, no 'at home' paradigms, 12 points sitting in boilerplate he can recite cold.
essays.habit: Write the four-line long-arm opener before you analyze anything: state statute must authorize, federal court borrows the state's long-arm, this one reaches the constitutional maximum, so the two prongs merge.

essays.model:
ANSWER TO QUESTION 2

1. ***Motion for summary judgment:*** The federal court properly granted Acme's motion for summary judgment on the failure to warn claim. In deciding whether to grant a motion for summary judgment, the court must determine whether a genuine dispute of material fact exists. In general, a summary judgment must be granted if, from the pleadings, affidavits, and discovery materials, it appears that there is no genuine dispute of material fact and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. If the moving party submits an affidavit or other evidence in support of the motion for summary judgment, the nonmoving party must counter that affidavit with his own evidence from affidavits, discovery, etc., on the matter. In the present case, Acme submitted affidavits from employees of both Acme (the manufacturer) and Widgets, Inc. (the distributor) stating that the widget had a proper warning attached when the widget was delivered to Widgets, and Plaintiff submitted an affidavit stating that the widget had no warning attached when she bought the widget from the retailer. It is important to note that, under state law, Acme's liability is discharged if a proper warning label was affixed when Acme delivered the widget to Widgets, Inc. Thus, although Plaintiff submitted her own affidavit in response to the motion for summary judgment, it did not address the relevant issue under state law—whether a proper warning was affixed when Acme delivered the widget to Widgets, its distributor. Therefore, on the evidence presented during the motion there was no genuine dispute of material fact, and Acme was entitled to a judgment as a matter of law. As a result, the federal court's ruling was proper.

2. ***Preclusive effect of federal court judgment:*** The State Y court should not give preclusive effect to the federal court judgment and should not dismiss Plaintiff's claim against Widgets. At issue is whether the state court should give preclusive effect (of either the claim or issue variety) to the federal court's rulings in *Plaintiff v. Acme*. First, Widgets is attempting to assert that Plaintiff's claim is barred by the disposition of the claims in *Plaintiff v. Acme*. For claim preclusion to apply, there must have been a valid, final judgment on the merits, ***both*** parties must be the same (or be in privity with a party in the prior suit), and the new action must involve the same cause of action, meaning that all claims must arise out of the same transaction or occurrence. Here, although the decision in *Plaintiff v. Acme* is a final judgment on the merits and the cause of action arose from the same transaction or occurrence, the parties are not the same, as Acme was being sued in the first case while Widgets is being sued in the second case, and there is no indication that Acme and Widgets are in privity. Thus, application of claim preclusion would be inappropriate.

Next, Widgets is also claiming that the federal court has already ruled in *Plaintiff v. Acme* that a proper warning had been affixed to the widget. For issue preclusion to apply, the issues in both actions must be the same, there must have been a final judgment as to that issue, the party against whom collateral estoppel is asserted must have had a fair opportunity to be heard on the matter, and the posture of the case must be such that it would not be unfair or inequitable to apply collateral estoppel. In *Plaintiff v. Widgets*, it is the first element that is lacking. In *Plaintiff v. Acme*, the issue was whether a proper warning had been affixed when Acme delivered the widget to Widgets, the distributor. In *Plaintiff v. Widgets*, the issue is whether a proper warning had been affixed when Widgets delivered the widget to the retailer. Therefore, an affidavit (or discovery) will have to be obtained from the retailer. If the retailer states that the warning was affixed, Widgets will be able to make a motion for summary judgment, much like Acme did in the first case, because under state law a distributor's duty is discharged if a warning label was affixed when the product was delivered to the retailer. If the retailer states that the warning was not affixed, Plaintiff will be able to survive any motion for summary judgment, as there would be a genuine dispute of material fact for the jury to decide. However, because the issues are not the same, use of issue preclusion would be inappropriate.

As to the dangerous defect claim, no judicial finding was ever made, as the case was settled out of court. Because settlements do not involve actual litigation, and generally do not involve any admissions of liablity, they do not have issue preclusive effect. As a result, Widgets cannot use the judgment by settlement against Plaintiff (even if the settlement could be perceived as a negative event to Plaintiff).

essays.answer:
1. JMOL Proper?

The issue is whether the corproation's motion for judgement as a matter of law (JMOL) was procedurally proper. A JMOL is procedurally improper where the moving-party brings their motion before the non-moving party has "had an opportunity to be heard." Likewise, if the JMOL is filed after the plaintiff's close of evidence, the motion is procedurally proepr - whether or not it is likely to succeed. 

Here, Corporation moved for JMOL at the close of Plaintiff's evidence. This fact means that the due process requirement was satisfied, since Plaintiff had an opportuntiy for their case to be heard. While the motion was denied, it was nevertheless procedurally proper. 

2. Grant post-judgement JMOL? 

The issue is whether a judge's beleif that the moving-party's evidence was "more credible and persuasive" is sufficient to grant a post-judgement JMOL. In the event that the moving-party has properly preserved the opportunity to bring a post-judgement JMOL, they must do so at the close of trial. The post-judgement motion only preserves the issues orignially brought during trial in the original JMOL. A post-judgement JMOL will be granted for any issues preserved during trial. A post-judgement JMOL removes relieves the moving-party of the judgement imposed in the prior pending action. This is a substantial form of relief that is only imposed where the moving-party demonstrates, based on all of the evidence presented in their case, which is viewed in a light most favorable to the non-moving party, that a reasonable jury could not have supplied the veridct that was given based on the evidence in the case. 

Here, the Corporation's post-judement JMOl merely argues the evidence presented at trial was "more persuasive and more credible" than Plaintiff's evidence. This fact is important, since it falls well-below the standard the court applies when assessing whether a post-judgement JMOL should be imposed. Even where a judge agrees that the evidence may have been more persuasive, that leaves open a possibility that a jury could have reasonably disagreed based on the evidence presented. Further, the Corporation's additional claim in their post-judgement JMOL (alleging that a jury foreperson failed to disclose involvement in prior disputes) was not preserved in their original JMOL, and therefore cannot serve as a basis for the court's consideration. 

Because of the constitutional burden imposed by a post-judgement JMOL on the non-moving party, and the insufficiency of evidence presented in the corproation's motion to meet the motion's strict requirements that must be satisfied in order to be granted, the post-judgement JMOL should be dismissed. 

3. Motion for new trial: "more persuasive and credible"

The issue is whether the corporation's argument that their evidence was more persuasive and creidble than the Plaintiff's is sufficient to grant a new trial. While a motion for new trial does not impose the same constitutional burden on the non-moving party, and therefore has a lower barrier to relief than a post-judgement JMOL, a motion for a new trial may not be granted where there is simply no evidence that the jury verdict is "unconscionable," nor any other circumstances affecting the proceedings, imposed a finding that some circumstances were such that imposition of the judgement on the moving-party is substantially unfair or affects the interests of justice. 

Here, the Corporation argues that a new trial should be granted because their evidence was more persuasive and more credible than the Plaintiffs. While this may be true, it leaves open a possibility that a reasonable jury could disagree. Juries often arrive at disagreeable verdicts, but such verdicts do not warrant retrial unless the jury's verdict "shocks the conscience" such that imposition of the verdict be against the courts interests of fairness. Further, the defendant does not argue the merits of their motion with any specificity, so it would be difficult for the court to consider whether the credibility issue may warrant a retrial to begin with. 

Because the corporation has not demonstrated that the verdict was substantially unfair or unconscionable, the motion for retrial on these grounds should be denied.

4. Motion for new trial: "foreperson's conduct"

However, the court should grant the motion for a new trial based on the foreperson's conduct. A federal court may grant a party's motion for retrial where a juryperson concealed facts that sufficiently warrant concerns for juror bias.

Here, the juror had stated that they planned to "stick it to the Corporation" and "teach tehse companies not to discriminate." This fact is critical, because the juror has expressly admitted that they had an egregious bias against one of the parties to the suit. Moreover, the juror was not honest during voir dire when asked whether she had been a party to an emplyoment discrimination lawsuit. In fact, she had been a party to two prior employment discrimination suits, which she brought herself. While this fact, alone, is insufficient, the fact that she intentionally concealed it demonstrates a clear bias warranting retrial.
essays.model:
1. ***Procedure for renewed JMOL:*** Corporation's renewed motion for judgment as a matter of law ("JMOL") was not procedurally proper, in that it raised new grounds in the motion. In determining whether to grant a renewed judgment as a matter of law, the court must determine whether the party previously moved for a JMOL, and what the grounds for the previous motion were. Under the federal rules, a judgment as a matter of law must be made at some point during the trial. A party also is limited to the grounds raised in the initial JMOL. (In other words, a party is unable to "renew" an objection that was not raised in the initial motion, as there would be no objection to renew.) The party also must make the renewed motion for JMOL within 28 days of the judgment. In the instant case, this means that the post-judgment JMOL arguably was timely made, in that some JMOL motion was made during the trial and Corporation is still within the 28-day window. However, the facts also indicate that the basis for Corporation's motion was that its evidence was more persuasive and more credible than that of the plaintiff. Obviously, given that Corporation moved for a JMOL at the close of the ***plaintiff's*** case, the defendant had not yet presented any evidence. Thus, the post-verdict motion for JMOL raised new grounds—Corporation could not have argued at the close of the plaintiff's case that its evidence was more persuasive, because it had not presented that evidence yet. As a result, it would be procedurally improper to consider that argument after the verdict is reached, as Corporation attempted to "renew" a motion that was never presented to the court in the first place.

2. ***Substance of renewed JMOL:*** Even if the motion was procedurally proper, the court probably should not grant Corporation's motion for JMOL. At issue is when the court may overturn the jury's verdict when ruling on a motion for a renewed JMOL. To grant a motion for JMOL or a renewed motion for JMOL, the court must find that a reasonable jury would not have a legally sufficient basis to find for the party on the issue. The court must view the evidence in a light most favorable to the nonmoving party and without considering the credibility of witnesses. The facts indicate that Plaintiff called a witness who heard Plaintiff's supervisor say that women were unsuited for management work. The facts also imply that Plaintiff submitted other evidence. Given the high hurdle that must be reached before taking a case from the jury, this evidence likely would be sufficient to defeat a motion or renewed motion for JMOL. As a result, even if the motion were procedurally proper, it should not be granted for the substantive grounds as described above. (*Note:* The juror misconduct would not be a reason to grant judgment in favor of the losing party; rather, a new trial would be the appropriate remedy, as discussed below.)

3. ***Motion for new trial based on evidence:*** The court should not grant a motion for a new trial on the ground that Corporation's evidence was more persuasive and credible than Plaintiff's evidence. In determining whether to grant a new trial, the issue becomes how much weight to give to the jury's verdict. Generally, a new trial may be granted because of some serious error that occurred during the trial (for example, an error in the admission of evidence, error in instructing the jury, the verdict is excessive, etc.). In theory, a new trial could be granted if the jury's verdict represents a serious error of judgment, but the judge may not replace the jury verdict with the verdict he would have reached. On the evidence of the case, it is not clear that a serious error has resulted from the jury's verdict. Plaintiff must have presented some substantial evidence, because the judge refused to grant a motion for JMOL at the close of Plaintiff's case. As a result, the jury's verdict should not be overturned lightly, at least not because the judge would not have reached the same verdict. Therefore, the court should not grant a motion for a new trial on the ground that Corporation's evidence was more persuasive and credible than Plaintiff's evidence.

4. ***Motion for new trial based on juror misconduct:*** The court should grant Corporation's motion for a new trial because of the jury foreperson's misconduct, both for failing to disclose her participation in two prior discrimination lawsuits and for having an actual bias against Corporation. At issue is whether alleged juror bias and nondisclosure of information are grounds for a new trial. The rule for granting new trials based on juror bias or misconduct is essentially the same as described in 3., above. In the instant case, the jury foreperson failed to inform the court that she had previously filed and lost two employment discrimination lawsuits. This factor alone, without any other showing of actual bias, probably would have been sufficient to have her disqualified for cause. (It is unlikely that she could have put aside her two losses when hearing the same type of case without prejudging the matter.) The fact that she made statements to the effect that she was out to get Corporation further buttresses this position, in that her failure to disclose may have been outright lying rather than a mere oversight, which shows her actual and unfair bias against Corporation. She also was the jury foreperson, giving her the position to possibly influence the jury to an even greater degree. Given this taint, the jury's verdict probably was unfairly compromised, thus entitling Corporation to a new trial.
